def: The version of IELTS for people applying to study at university or to register in some professions. Reading and Writing use academic texts and tasks.
The version used for work, migration and some schools and training programmes. Reading uses everyday and workplace texts, and Writing Task 1 is a letter.
Results are given on a scale from 0 to 9, in half bands such as 6.5. Each of the four skills gets a band, and there is an overall band.
The average of the four skill bands, rounded to the nearest half band. An average ending in .25 rounds up to .5, and one ending in .75 rounds up to the next whole band.
The number of correct answers out of 40 in Listening or Reading. It is converted to a band using a table that can vary slightly between test versions.
The official results document, showing the band for each skill and the overall band.
IELTS taken on a computer at a test centre. Paper-based IELTS is being withdrawn around mid-2026, with dates that vary by country.
A hybrid option offered in some places, where Listening and Reading are on computer but the two Writing tasks are handwritten.
An option in some places to retake just one of the four skills, instead of the whole test, within a set period after the original test.
A face-to-face or video-call conversation with an examiner, lasting 11 to 14 minutes in three parts. It may be on the same day as the other skills or up to about a week before or after.
In Speaking Part 2 you receive a task card, have one minute to prepare and make notes, and then speak for up to two minutes.
A report of at least 150 words describing a graph, table, chart, diagram, process or map. About 20 minutes is suggested.
A letter of at least 150 words responding to a situation, covering three bullet points. It may be formal, semi-formal or informal.
An essay of at least 250 words in response to a point of view, argument or problem. It is worth more than Task 1, and about 40 minutes is suggested.
The writing criterion about how fully and appropriately you answer the task. Task Achievement is used for Task 1 and Task Response for Task 2.
The writing and speaking criterion about how logically ideas are organised and linked.
The criterion about the range and accuracy of your vocabulary.
The criterion about the variety of your sentence structures and how correct they are.
The speaking criterion about speaking at length without long pauses, and organising what you say.
The speaking criterion about how easy you are to understand, including sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation. Accent itself is not penalised.
Instructions such as NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. An answer that breaks the limit is marked wrong even if it contains the right words.
In True/False/Not Given and Yes/No/Not Given questions, the answer when the text does not say whether the statement is true.
An answer option or a piece of information designed to look right but be wrong, such as a date a speaker mentions and then changes.
Saying the same idea in different words. IELTS questions usually paraphrase the text or recording rather than repeat it.
Versions of IELTS approved for some UK visa and immigration applications, taken at specially approved test centres.
The Common European Framework of Reference, a scale from A1 to C2 that IELTS bands can be broadly compared with.
A request, for a fee, to have a test re-marked. The fee is refunded if the score changes.
Most organisations accept IELTS results for two years, but each organisation sets its own rule.
